transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, what brings me in is... I've been working on this memorial for my brother, and it’s just gotten a lot bigger than I meant it to. 

I’ve been spending most of my days lately just chasing down the right songs, calling folks up, planning out displays and trips. It feels important to get it right, but my wife is pretty concerned. She says I’ve completely pushed aside the garden, my walking group, and just about everything else I normally do. So... she really wanted me to come talk to you about it.
Over these past weeks while you've been so focused on the memorial, have you noticed you're needing much less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm sleeping about the same amount I always do. I might wake up a bit early sometimes thinking about the displays or who I need to call next, but I wouldn't say I need less sleep. And I don't exactly feel full of energy... just, well, very focused on getting this done for him.
How long ago did your brother pass away, and when did you start feeling this intense pull to work on the memorial?

He passed away about two months ago. And... well, that's pretty much when all this started. I began working on his tribute right after we lost him, so this whole thing has been going on for about two months now.

When you think about the memorial throughout the day, do those thoughts feel unwanted or intrusive—like they force their way in and cause you distress—or do they feel more like a comforting way you want to spend your time thinking about your brother?

No, they don't feel unwanted at all. It's not like they force their way into my head and upset me or anything like that. 

I actually want to be thinking about it. It's... well, it's a way to feel close to him, I guess. I just want to make sure I do right by him, so spending my time on it feels like the right thing to do. It definitely doesn't cause me any distress to think about the memorial, it's just important to me.
Has this focus on the memorial caused ongoing tension or problems in your marriage or other relationships, or affected your ability to keep up with important responsibilities?

Well, yes, it has caused some problems. I suppose I've dropped a lot of my usual activities. I haven't been to my walking group or my book club in a while, and the garden is just completely overgrown at this point. 

And... well, I've upset some folks at the senior center. They say everything I talk about now is just the memorial display, and they get tired of it. As for my wife, she's definitely feeling the strain. She tells me that our whole day just revolves around trying to calm me down, or her trying to talk me out of making another phone call, or taking another trip for supplies, or getting into another argument with someone about it. So, yes, it's definitely affecting things.
Aside from how this has affected your relationships and activities, have you personally been feeling very sad, guilty, or hopeless since your brother passed away?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean... of course I miss him, but I haven't really been feeling sad or hopeless or anything like that. And I don't feel guilty, either. 

I guess most folks expect you to be sitting around crying when you lose a brother, but I haven't felt down. Mostly I just feel... well, driven to get this memorial finished. So no, I haven't had those kinds of feelings.
When your wife or others try to get you to slow down or stop working on the memorial, do you find yourself feeling unusually irritable, angry, or on edge with them?

Well, yeah, I do. I mean, I'll feel really... lit up, you know? Full of purpose one minute, thinking about how the whole town is finally going to understand our family when they see this. But then... yeah, if my wife or someone at the senior center tries to slow me down or questions what I'm doing with the display, I just snap at them. I get really irritable. It's like they're just getting in the way of what needs to be done.
Besides feeling driven to finish the memorial, have you noticed feeling unusually confident, special, or like you have grand plans or abilities that go beyond how you'd normally see yourself?

Well, I don't know about grand plans or feeling special, exactly. I mean, I just know this memorial is important and I'm the one who has to do it right. But I don't think I have any special powers or anything like that. I'm just focused on getting this done.
Have you noticed your thoughts racing or jumping quickly from one idea to another—more than you're used to—especially when you're working on the memorial?

Yeah, I definitely have. It's like... my mind just won't stop. It keeps jumping from one idea to the next. One minute I'm thinking about how to build a display case, and then suddenly I'm planning a road trip to find this cousin I haven't seen in years. And then, before I know it, I'm trying to remember a verse from some old ballad my brother liked. It all just comes so fast, and I can't even slow it down enough to write it all out in order. It's just... constant.
Over the past two months, has this heightened, irritable, 'lit up' feeling and drive to work on the memorial been present nearly every day for at least a full week at a time, without letting up?

I... I'm not really sure about that. I haven't exactly been keeping track of the days on a calendar or anything. I mean, it's been happening a lot lately, this whole drive to get it done, but I couldn't tell you if it's been every single day for a full week straight without a break. I just know I've been focused on it pretty heavy for a while now.

Before your brother passed away, had you ever gone through a period—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually high-energy, irritable, or 'lit up' like this, or a period of significant depression, at any other time in your life?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had times where I felt a little down, or times where I had some energy, just like anybody else. But nothing like this. Nothing that lasted for weeks or where I felt this... this driven, or this irritable. Before he passed, things were just pretty normal, really. I never had anything like what's happening right now.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits an elevated, irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity (memorial project), racing/flight of ideas, distractibility, irritability when interrupted, and significant functional impairment (withdrawal from usual activities, marital strain, social friction) persisting for about two months. Symptoms began after a bereavement but exceed normal grief reactions (thoughts are non-intrusive, ego-syntonic, and associated with pressured, expansive behavior rather than sadness or guilt). No prior manic or depressive episodes reported, making this a first manic episode. Because there is no history of a prior mood episode, this is best classified as F30.9 (Manic Episode, unspecified) rather than Bipolar Disorder. Grief-related diagnoses are excluded given the presence of core manic symptoms (flight of ideas, irritability, grandiosity-adjacent drive, risky goal-directed behavior) rather than depressive or intrusive grief symptoms.

confirmed_symptoms: Elevated/irritable mood ('lit up', irritable when interrupted)
Increased goal-directed activity (extensive memorial planning, calls, trips, displays)
Flight of ideas/racing thoughts (jumping between unrelated tasks rapidly)
Distractibility (unable to organize or write ideas in order)
Irritability when others try to slow him down
Increased involvement in activities with potential negative consequences (arguments, social friction, marital strain)
Denies intrusive or distressing quality of thoughts (ego-syntonic, not typical grief rumination)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms present for approximately 2 months since brother's death; patient unable to confirm continuous week-long duration but reports persistent, near-daily symptoms during this period.
additional_requirements: No prior history of manic, hypomanic, or depressive episodes confirmed
Symptoms not better explained by normal grief (non-intrusive, non-distressing, activity-driven rather than sadness-driven)
Significant impairment in social, marital, and community functioning confirmed
